segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 1: Week 32 Listening: A Data Review Meeting

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Hi, Tom. Thanks for coming in early. We need to go over the survey data before the team meeting at ten.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Sure, Mia. I printed the summary, but I noticed a few numbers look different from last month.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Right. The response rate was 68 percent this time, compared with 72 percent in March. That's a drop of four points.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Four points? That's not huge, but it's worth mentioning. Do you know why fewer people replied?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Possibly because we sent the survey on a Friday. Last time we sent it on a Tuesday.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: That makes sense. Friday is a bad day for office workers. So, what about the satisfaction score?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: The average score was 4.1 out of 5. In March it was 4.3. So it went down slightly.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Hmm. Still above four, which is good. But the drop is bigger than the response rate drop, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Yes, the satisfaction fell by 0.2 points, while the response rate fell by 4 percentage points. They are different units, so we can't compare them directly.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Good point. I almost made that mistake in my notes. Let me correct that.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Also, the number of comments increased. We received 156 comments this time, compared with 120 last time. That's 36 more.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: That's a lot of reading. Did you find any common themes?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Yes. The most frequent complaint was about the new booking system. About 40 percent of comments mentioned it.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Forty percent? That's nearly half. We should look into that.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Definitely. The second most common theme was staff friendliness, but those comments were mostly positive.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: OK. So the main problem is the booking system. What about the age groups?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: The 18 to 30 group had the lowest response rate, at 55 percent. The 31 to 50 group had the highest, at 78 percent.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: That's interesting. Maybe younger people prefer shorter surveys.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Possibly. We could test a shorter version next time. Now, about the retest phase.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Right, the phase retest. When do we need to finish it?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: The deadline is the 15th of next month. We need to collect at least 200 responses for the retest to be valid.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Two hundred. And how many do we have so far?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Only 85. So we need 115 more.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: That's a big gap. We should send a reminder next week.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Agreed. Also, remember that the retest will use the same questions as the first survey, so we can compare the results directly.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Good. I'll update the tracking sheet and send it to you by Thursday.

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Perfect. Let's meet again on Friday to check the progress.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Friday at two?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Yes, Friday at two works for me. Thanks, Tom.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 2: Data, Decisions, and the Museum's Visitor Survey

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Hello, everyone. My name is Sarah Chen, and I'm the visitor services manager at the Riverside Community Museum. Today I want to talk about how we use data from our visitor surveys to make better decisions. This is a simulated talk for educational purposes.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: First, let me give you some background. We started collecting survey data three years ago. In the first year, we had about 1,200 responses. Last year, that number rose to 3,500. That's almost three times more than the first year. But more importantly, we changed the way we ask questions.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Originally, we asked visitors to rate their overall experience on a scale from one to five. The average was 4.2, which seemed good. However, when we looked at the comments, we noticed something interesting. Many people wrote that they loved the exhibitions but found the café too expensive. So we decided to ask more specific questions.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, we ask about different areas separately: exhibitions, café, shop, and facilities. This year, the exhibitions scored 4.5, the café 3.8, the shop 4.1, and the facilities 4.3. As you can see, the café is still the lowest, but it has improved from 3.5 last year. That's a significant change.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: We also collect demographic information. For example, we ask about age groups. The largest group is people aged 35 to 54, making up 40 percent of visitors. Families with children under 12 are 25 percent. Students are 20 percent, and retirees are 15 percent. This helps us plan events. For instance, we now offer more family workshops on weekends because that group is growing.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Another thing we track is how people hear about us. Word of mouth is the most common, at 45 percent. Social media is 30 percent, and local newspapers are 15 percent. The remaining 10 percent comes from other sources. This tells us that we should invest more in social media, as it is growing fast.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: One challenge is that not everyone answers all questions. Some people skip the demographic section. We have to be careful not to assume that the people who answer are the same as those who don't. For example, younger visitors might be less likely to fill in paper surveys, so we now offer an online version as well.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, we use the data to set targets. Next year, we aim to increase overall satisfaction from 4.2 to 4.4. We also want to raise the café score to 4.0. And we plan to increase survey responses by 20 percent. These targets are ambitious but achievable if we work together.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Thank you for listening. If you have any questions, please feel free to ask.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 3: Data Interpretation and Stage Re-test

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good morning, both. Thanks for coming. Today we’re going to look at your data interpretation from the pilot study and then plan the stage re-test. Let’s start with the graphs you produced. Mia, can you talk us through the first chart?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Yes. This bar chart shows the number of students who completed the online module in three different weeks. Week one had the highest number—about 120 students. Week two dropped to 80, and week three was slightly lower, at 75. So the trend is downward after the first week.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Right. And what might explain that drop?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Possibly the deadline for another assignment. But I’m not sure—we didn’t collect data on that.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good point. We must be careful not to infer causes without evidence. Now, Leo, your line graph shows something different, doesn’t it?

segments.speaker: LEO
segments.text: Yes. My graph tracks the average score on the weekly quiz. It went up from 60% in week one to 75% in week two, then fell to 65% in week three. So it’s not a steady increase.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Exactly. So the two graphs tell different stories. Mia’s shows participation falling, while Leo’s shows performance rising then falling. This is why we need to compare carefully. Now, let’s think about the re-test. When should we run it?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: I think after week four, because by then students will have covered all the material.

segments.speaker: LEO
segments.text: But if we wait until week four, we might lose some participants. Maybe week three is better.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: There’s a trade-off. A later test gives a fuller picture, but risks lower attendance. Let’s note both options. Now, about the sample size: Mia, how many students took part in the pilot?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: Fifty? No, wait—it was sixty. I remember because we had three groups of twenty.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Correct, sixty. That’s a relatively small sample, so we shouldn’t generalise too much. Leo, what about the questionnaire response rate?

segments.speaker: LEO
segments.text: We sent it to all sixty, but only forty-five returned it. So the response rate was 75%.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Good. Now, for the re-test, we need to decide which questions to keep. Some items were too easy—almost everyone got them right. Others were too hard. We want a balanced test. Any suggestions?

segments.speaker: Mia
segments.text: We could remove the three easiest items and replace them with slightly harder ones.

segments.speaker: LEO
segments.text: Or we could keep them but add more challenging questions at the end.

segments.speaker: TUTOR
segments.text: Both are reasonable. Let’s aim for a test that takes about 30 minutes, no more. And remember to check the instructions carefully—last time some students misunderstood the scale. Okay, I think we have a plan. Let’s meet again next Tuesday to finalise the questions.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Section 4: Simulated Lecture: Understanding Data and Stage Re-testing

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about two connected ideas: how we understand data, and why we re-test at different stages. This is especially important for students who are learning to interpret numbers and graphs.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: First, let's think about what data actually is. Data is not just numbers. It includes any information we collect—words, images, measurements, even sounds. When we analyse data, we look for patterns. But patterns can be misleading if we are not careful. For example, a graph might show that sales increased after a new advertisement. But that does not prove the advertisement caused the increase. Maybe the season changed, or maybe a competitor closed. So we must ask: what else could explain this pattern?

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Now, let's move to stage re-testing. Why do we test at different stages? One reason is to check progress. If you learn something new, you need to see if you can still remember it a week later. This is called retention. A second reason is to find gaps. Maybe you understood the first part of a topic, but the second part is still unclear. Re-testing helps you identify those gaps.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: There are different types of re-testing. One type is immediate re-testing, right after learning. Another is delayed re-testing, perhaps a week or a month later. Research suggests that delayed re-testing often leads to better long-term memory. But immediate re-testing can still be useful for feedback.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: When you re-test, you should compare your results with your previous results. This is where data understanding comes in. You need to look at the numbers carefully. For instance, if your score went from 60 to 75, that is an improvement. But you should also consider the difficulty of the test. A harder test might give a lower score even if you have improved. So always ask: are these two tests comparable?

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Another point is about sample size. If you only test a few people, the results might not be reliable. A larger sample gives more trustworthy data. But even with a large sample, you must check for bias. For example, if you only test students who volunteer, they might not represent all students.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Finally, let's think about how to present data clearly. Use simple graphs and avoid too many colours. Label your axes. And always explain what the data shows in plain language. Remember, the goal is understanding, not just collecting numbers.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: To sum up, understanding data means asking critical questions about patterns and causes. Stage re-testing helps you track progress and find gaps. Combine the two, and you can make better decisions about your learning.
